title: Slope of a tangent line
goal: Watch the average slope between two points on a curve turn into the exact slope at a single point (the tangent line) as the second point slides into the first.

beforeThis.skill: Quick check: slope between two points is always $\frac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$, and the line through $(x_0, y_0)$ with slope $m$ is $y = y_0 + m(x - x_0)$.

seeIt.title: The paradox of the derivative (Ch. 2 of Essence of Calculus)
seeIt.creator: 3Blue1Brown
seeIt.watchFor: Shows how a secant slope between two nearby points becomes the tangent slope at a single point.

questions.asking: Find the sign (positive or negative) of the slope of the line connecting the peak $P$ to a point $Q$ on either side of the $y$-axis.
questions.statement: Shown below is the graph $y = f(x)$. If we choose a point $Q$ on the graph to the left of the $y$-axis, is the slope of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ positive or negative? If we choose a point $Q$ on the graph to the right of the $y$-axis, is the slope of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ positive or negative?

figures.alt: Graph of y = f(x) with a sharp highest point P on the positive y-axis. The curve rises concave up from the left toward P and falls concave up to the right of P.

questions.asking: Use the upward-bending curve to decide how moving $Q$ affects the secant slope through $P$ and $Q$, and compare that secant slope to the tangent slope at $P$.
questions.statement:
Shown below is the graph $y = f(x)$.

  1. If we want the slope of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ to increase, should we slide $Q$ closer to $P$, or further away?
  2. Which is larger, the slope of the tangent line at $P$, or the slope of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$?

figures.alt: Graph of an increasing, concave-up curve y = f(x) with point Q in the third quadrant and point P higher up in the first quadrant.

questions.asking: Sort the six graphs into groups that share the same secant line slope between $x = -2$ and $x = 2$.
questions.statement: Group the functions below into collections whose secant lines from $x = -2$ to $x = 2$ all have the same slopes.

figures.alt: Six small graphs labeled (a) through (f) over the interval from x = -2 to x = 2: (a) rises linearly from negative at x = -2 to positive at x = 2; (b) falls linearly from positive at x = -2 to lower positive at x = 2; (c) piecewise linear starting and ending on the x-axis at x = -2 and x = 2; (d) horizontal line from x = -2 to x = 2; (e) rises linearly with the same endpoints at x = -2 and x = 2 as (a); (f) trough-shaped piecewise linear graph starting and ending at the same height at x = -2 and x = 2.

questions.asking: Pick two grid points on the drawn tangent line and calculate rise over run ($\Delta y / \Delta x$) to estimate the slope at $x = 5$.
questions.statement: Give your best approximation of the slope of the tangent line to the graph below at the point $x = 5$.

figures.alt: Grid showing a smooth increasing curve. Grid major units are marked at 1 and 5 on the x-axis and 1 on the y-axis, with 5 subdivisions per unit. At x = 5, the curve passes near y = 0.5 and rises steeply from about y = 0 at x = 4 to y = 2 at x = 6.

questions.asking: Draw the tangent line at $P$ and pick any two points $Q$ and $R$ on the curve whose connecting secant line is parallel to that tangent line.
questions.statement: On the graph below, sketch the tangent line to $y = f(x)$ at $P$. Then, find two points $Q$ and $R$ on the graph so that the secant line through $Q$ and $R$ has the same slope as the tangent line at $P$.

figures.alt: Graph of a smooth curve y = f(x) dipping below the x-axis to a minimum near the y-axis and then rising to the right, with a point P marked just to the right of the minimum.

questions.asking: Spot every peak, valley, or flat shelf on the curve where a tangent line would sit completely flat (slope $= 0$).
questions.statement:
Mark the points where the curve shown below has a tangent line with slope $0$.

(Later on, we’ll learn how these points tell us a lot about the shape of a graph.)

figures.alt: Graph of a smooth curve y = f(x) that descends from the left, levels off briefly at a flat terrace in the second quadrant, continues down to a valley minimum on the negative y-axis, rises to a rounded peak in the fourth quadrant, and then descends.
